passage:
Coach's note, college pool. Devika Nair, 3 October
Wasim trained with the 6 am group every weekday until his exams in August. Since then he hasn't been back. His locker still has his goggles and towel in it; I checked because the cleaners asked.
Today I passed him near the canteen. He saw me, went red and suddenly became very interested in his phone. When I said hello, he said, "Sorry, ma'am, I've been meaning to come. Next week, pakka." He said the same thing two weeks ago.
His friend Aman tells me Wasim changes the subject whenever swimming comes up and has stopped sitting at the café near the pool.
I don't think he's lazy. He looks embarrassed, as if coming back means facing how much ground he's lost.
What I did next: I sent him a short message. "No catching up needed. Just come on Friday and float for fifteen minutes. Your goggles are waiting."

qa.q: What is still in Wasim's locker?
qa.a: His goggles and towel.

qa.q: Why might Wasim go red and look at his phone when he sees the coach?
qa.a: He seems ashamed of not coming back, and seeing the coach reminds him of a goal he feels he has failed.

qa.q: Why does Devika's message fit this stage?
qa.a: It removes the pressure to catch up and asks only for fifteen minutes of floating, so restarting doesn't feel like facing a failure.

qa.q: What might Aman notice about Wasim?
qa.a: Aman sees Wasim dodge any talk of swimming and avoid the café near the pool, and may be puzzled or worried by the change.

grounding: Shows a young adult avoiding a lapsed swimming routine and the coach, with shame making the return feel like confronting failure.

passage:
Sunday
The Spanish notebook is still on my desk under a pile of laundry, which is exactly where I put it so I wouldn't have to see it.
Twenty-three days since my last lesson. The app sent a reminder this morning and I swiped it away so fast.
At lunch Zubin asked, "How's the Spanish going? Say something!" I laughed, said "Hola", and asked about his internship before he could ask anything else. My face was burning.
I told everyone in July I'd be conversational by Diwali. Now opening that notebook feels like opening a report card I already know is bad. Every day I don't start, it gets heavier.
Maybe tomorrow. I wrote that yesterday too.
Ritu

qa.q: Where is Ritu's Spanish notebook?
qa.a: On the desk under a pile of laundry.

qa.q: Why did Ritu's face burn when Zubin asked about the Spanish?
qa.a: Ritu felt ashamed of having stopped after telling everyone about being conversational by Diwali, so the question felt like being found out.

qa.q: What small step could break the avoidance?
qa.a: Ritu could uncover the notebook and do one short lesson without trying to catch up, or tell Zubin honestly about the break and ask for company.

qa.q: What might Zubin have noticed at lunch?
qa.a: Zubin was probably just curious and friendly, and may have noticed the quick 'Hola' and change of subject without knowing the shame behind it.

grounding: Illustrates a neglected learning habit, a hidden notebook and dodged questions, where shame makes restarting feel like facing a bad report card.

passage:
So your roommate has stopped her morning runs, and you keep reminding her? Afreen, beta, let me tell you about your Jagdish Nana's own mistake.
When I was twenty, in the Allahabad hostel, my roommate Mohan started doing yoga every morning. Proud as anything. Then exams came, he stopped, and his mat sat rolled up in the corner.
I thought I was helping. Every morning: "Mohan, the mat is waiting! Mohan, where's your discipline?" He started sleeping later just to avoid me. Once he kicked the mat under the bed. The more I pushed, the less he did.
One day I got tired of my own voice. I spread my towel next to his bed and said, "I'm doing ten minutes of stretching. Join if you want, no big deal."
He grumbled. Then he joined. Ten minutes became a habit for both of us.
So, beta, try that.

qa.q: What did Jagdish say to Mohan every morning at first?
qa.a: "Mohan, the mat is waiting! Mohan, where's your discipline?"

qa.q: Why did Mohan start sleeping later?
qa.a: He likely felt pressured and ashamed by the daily reminders, so he avoided Jagdish and the mat.

qa.q: What changed when Jagdish stopped nagging?
qa.a: He did his own ten minutes of stretching and simply invited Mohan to join, which made restarting light instead of a confrontation.

qa.q: What might Afreen's roommate be feeling after days of reminders?
qa.a: The roommate may feel judged and embarrassed about the stopped runs, and each reminder may make going back harder, just as it did for Mohan.

grounding: Shows a roommate's nagging hardening avoidance of a lapsed routine, and a relaxed ten-minute invitation making the restart feel easy.

The power had been out since seven, and the tiny Koramangala flat was hot and dark. By phone torchlight Jahnavi could see Rafiq's running shoes by the door, laces tucked in, exactly where they had been for three weeks.
"You know those shoes are just decoration now," she said. "You told everyone you'd run the 10K in December."
Rafiq didn't answer. He turned to the wall and stayed there, scrolling. The next morning he left for work early, stepping round the shoes.
Jahnavi felt bad. That evening, with the power still flickering, she tried again, softer. "I'm walking to the lake for ten minutes before it gets dark. Want to come? Walking only. Shoes optional."
Rafiq hesitated, then reached for the shoes. "Ten minutes," he said. "Walking."
On the way back, he jogged the last block without a word.

qa.q: How long had Rafiq's running shoes been by the door?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq turn to the wall after Jahnavi's first comment?
qa.a: The dig about the shoes and the 10K probably made him feel ashamed and pressured, so he shut down and avoided the subject.

qa.q: What made Jahnavi's second approach work?
qa.a: She offered a short, easy walk with no expectations, 'shoes optional', which made restarting feel light instead of like facing a failure.

qa.q: What might Rafiq be experiencing as he jogs the last block?
qa.a: He may feel relief and quiet pride at moving again, without the weight of explaining himself or promising anything.

grounding: Illustrates a flatmate whose teasing about a neglected routine deepens avoidance, and whose calm offer to walk for ten minutes eases the restart.

Siddharth had tried waking at five to exercise three times this year, and three times he had given up by the second week. Sitting on the step outside his rented room in Hoshangabad, he finally made a different plan.
Not an hour of exercise. Ten squats while the milk heated for his morning tea, because the milk heated every morning anyway. And instead of taking the tempo right to the cooperative bank, he would get off at the Sethani Ghat stop and walk the last stretch along the river. He even left his walking chappals by the door, facing out.
His colleague Pradeep, who shared the tempo, laughed. "Ten squats? That's not exercise, that's stretching."
"It's ten more than last month," Siddharth said.
By the third week he was doing twenty, and Pradeep had started getting off at Sethani Ghat too.

qa.q: Where does Siddharth get off the tempo now?
qa.a: At the Sethani Ghat stop.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth decide against waking at five again?
qa.a: He had given up three times by the second week, so he seems to believe a big plan that depends on motivation won't work for him.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Tying ten squats to heating the milk and walking from Sethani Ghat linked exercise to things he already did, and the chappals by the door removed friction.

qa.q: How does Pradeep's view of the plan change?
qa.a: Pradeep first laughs that ten squats is just stretching, but by the third week is getting off at Sethani Ghat too.

grounding: Illustrates redesigning an exercise habit into a tiny version tied to tea and the commute, with less friction, rather than relying on motivation.

passage:
Aadhya came home from her cousin's sangeet at 2 am, heels in hand, and fell asleep without her usual fifteen minutes of sitar practice. It was the first miss in seven weeks.
The next morning in their Andheri flat, Ira found her tuning the sitar at 7:30 as usual.
"Doing double today to make up?" Ira asked, pouring tea.
"Nope. Just fifteen minutes."
"No guilt trip?"
Aadhya shrugged. "Yesterday I was at a sangeet till two. That's what happened, not what I am."
She scribbled a line in her small practice notebook: "Missed, late function. Next time, five minutes before leaving." Then she played her fifteen minutes, a little rusty, and got ready for work.
Ira noticed she was still humming the raag as she packed her lunch.

qa.q: How long does Aadhya usually practise the sitar?
qa.a: Her usual fifteen minutes of sitar practice.

qa.q: What does Aadhya mean by 'That's what happened, not what I am'?
qa.a: She sees the miss as a fact about one late night, not proof that she is weak or undisciplined.

qa.q: Why is Aadhya's line in the practice notebook useful?
qa.a: It treats the slip as information, noting the reason and a plan for next time, instead of punishing herself with double practice.

qa.q: What does Ira expect, and what does Ira see instead?
qa.a: Ira expects double practice or a guilt trip, but sees an ordinary fifteen minutes and Aadhya humming the raag, calm about the miss.

grounding: Shows a young adult restarting practice the day after a miss without penance, treating the slip as information rather than a flaw.

"No walk yesterday, Saurabh bhaiya?" Chetan grinned from the sofa. "Streak broken! Forty-two days gone!"
Saurabh laced his shoes. "It rained like crazy. I'm going today."
"Aren't you doing two rounds to make up?" Maa called from the kitchen.
"No, Maa. One round, same as always."
"So yesterday is just... lost?" Chetan asked.
"Yesterday was rain. It's not proof I'm lazy. The rule is just: never two days in a row."
Papa lowered the newspaper. "When I gave up smoking, I slipped once at a wedding. Told myself I'd failed and bought a packet the next day. It took me another year."
Saurabh paused at the door. "That's exactly what I don't want."
"Go, go," Papa said. "And take the umbrella."
Chetan was already pulling on his chappals. "Wait. I'm coming. One round."

qa.q: Why did Saurabh miss his walk yesterday?
qa.a: It rained like crazy.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh pause at the door after Papa's story?
qa.a: He recognised that treating one slip as total failure had cost Papa a year, and he wants to avoid that same trap.

qa.q: What rule does Saurabh use, and why does it help?
qa.a: Never two days in a row: he restarts with one ordinary round the next day, so the slip stays small instead of becoming a reason to quit.

qa.q: What does Papa's story show about how he sees slips now?
qa.a: Papa has learned from his own lost year that calling one slip a failure can undo progress, so he backs Saurabh going out today.

grounding: Illustrates restarting a walking habit the day after a miss with no make-up rounds, treating the slip as a one-off rather than proof of weakness.

passage:
Running club notes. Saurabh Joshi, coach. Saturday, 18 January
Sonali has run with the Saturday group since last April. At first she needed a reminder every Friday night. Now I don't think she even decides; she just turns up at 6:15, stretches by the same lamppost and asks who's pacing.
In December she missed three Saturdays while her father was in hospital. I half expected her to drop off, as many do. Instead she came back on the fourth, ran an easy 4 km at the back and said, "Felt weird not running. Like skipping brushing my teeth." She didn't apologise or promise to make up the distance.
She mentioned she expects to miss more when her new job starts in March. "I'll just come back when I can," she said, and went to find her water bottle.
What I did next: moved her to the easier group for two weeks without comment, and noted a check-in for March.

qa.q: How many Saturdays did Sonali miss in December?
qa.a: She missed three Saturdays.

qa.q: What does Sonali's 'Like skipping brushing my teeth' reveal about how running feels to her now?
qa.a: Running needs little thought and feels odd to skip, so it has become an ordinary part of her life.

qa.q: How did the coach support Sonali's return, and why does it fit?
qa.a: Saurabh moved her to an easier group for two weeks without comment and planned a March check-in, letting her come back without drama.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel seeing Sonali return?
qa.a: Saurabh half expected her to drop off, as many do, so the calm return is likely a relief and a sign the habit has taken root.

grounding: Shows a running habit that has become automatic after months, with the runner expecting lapses and returning calmly after a disruption.

passage:
Thursday, 9 pm
Back on the cycle today after nine days. The house shifting swallowed everything: boxes, the broker, the new gas connection, Usha's mother visiting. The cycle sat in the new building's parking under a bedsheet.
Funny thing is, I didn't sit down and plan a restart. This morning I just found myself pumping the tyres before chai, as if my hands had decided. Eight months ago I needed three alarms and a pep talk to do this ride.
The new route is longer, past the lake and under the flyover. My legs were heavy but I didn't mind much.
All nine days felt slightly off, like I'd forgotten something. Usha said I was grumpy. Probably true.
I know there'll be more gaps. Her sister's wedding in May, for one. Fine. The cycle will be there.
Vishal

qa.q: How many days was Vishal off the cycle?
qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: How did the nine days without cycling feel to Vishal, and what does that suggest?
qa.a: They felt slightly off, like something was forgotten, which suggests cycling has become a background habit that feels strange to skip.

qa.q: What in Vishal's attitude helps the habit survive future gaps?
qa.a: Vishal expects gaps like the May wedding and plans simply to return, instead of treating a break as failure.

qa.q: How might Usha have experienced those nine days?
qa.a: Usha, busy with the move and her mother's visit, found Vishal grumpy, and may be glad to see the cycle back in use.

grounding: Illustrates a months-old cycling habit that returns almost automatically after a house move, with future lapses expected and accepted.

passage:
My sister Madhuri started learning to swim at twenty-five, and I've watched her go about it very differently from me. I'm Vandana, the one who buys a new planner every January and abandons it by February.
Madhuri just keeps a small card on the fridge. After each swim she draws a dot. No numbers, no streak counter. When I asked why, she said, "I'm counting swims, not days in a row."
Every Sunday, if there are three dots that week, she buys herself filter coffee at the corner shop. Not for a perfect week. For three swims.
The part that surprised me: before her first week, she wrote on the card, "Bad day plan: go, get in, float five minutes, come home." Last Thursday she had a migraine and a deadline, and I watched her do exactly that.
I can't know what she felt. She looked tired, but not defeated.

qa.q: What does Madhuri draw after each swim?
qa.a: A dot on a small card on the fridge.

qa.q: What does Madhuri's 'I'm counting swims, not days in a row' suggest about her thinking?
qa.a: She wants to value each swim rather than a perfect streak, so a missed day won't feel like losing everything.

qa.q: Why was Madhuri's bad-day plan useful last Thursday?
qa.a: Because it was written in advance, she could do a small version, five minutes of floating, on a hard day, so the habit carried on.

qa.q: How does watching Madhuri affect Vandana?
qa.a: Vandana, who abandons planners by February, is surprised by the calm approach and seems to be seeing a different way to build a habit.

grounding: Shows light tracking, rewards for doing rather than for streaks, and a bad-day plan set in advance so one hard day doesn't break the habit.

Day 1, a Monday. Simran, a night-shift nurse in Ludhiana, bought a thin notebook to learn Gurmukhi calligraphy, ten letters a day. On the first page she wrote two rules: tick the day in pencil, nothing fancier; and after every tenth practice, one jalebi from the sweet shop near the hospital.
"Ten practices, not ten days in a row?" her roommate Rekha asked.
"Doing it is the point," Simran said.
Day 16. Fourteen pencil ticks, two gaps, two jalebis eaten. Simran felt proud and a little smug. That evening she added a line at the back: "Bad shift plan: write one letter. Just one."
Day 23. After a twelve-hour shift with two emergencies, she came home grey-faced. Rekha watched her open the notebook, carefully write one letter, tick the day and go to sleep.
The next evening she was back to ten.

qa.q: What reward did Simran give herself after every tenth practice?
qa.a: One jalebi from the sweet shop near the hospital.

qa.q: Why did Simran say 'Doing it is the point'?
qa.a: She wanted to reward the practice itself rather than a perfect streak, so gaps wouldn't spoil her pride in learning.

qa.q: What made the bad-shift plan work on Day 23?
qa.a: She had decided in advance to write just one letter on a bad day, so she could keep going even while exhausted, and she was back to ten the next evening.

qa.q: What might Rekha take from watching Simran on Day 23?
qa.a: Rekha, who questioned the 'ten practices' rule, sees how a small plan let Simran keep the habit on a terrible day without guilt 🙂.

grounding: Illustrates tracking a new habit lightly, rewarding practice rather than a streak, and a pre-planned bad-day version that keeps a miss from breaking it.

passage:
Monday. Rashmi's first month at the new school in Pune, and lunch was still the worst part. She ate on the library steps, pretending to read. That night she downloaded an online strategy game her cousin had mentioned, just to see what it was like.
Saturday. She played for four hours straight. Yash, her friend from her old school in Nagpur, was on it too and kept teaming up with her, typing "nice save!" For the first time in weeks her chest didn't feel tight. When Mummy called her for dinner she said, "Five minutes," and it felt like a hiding place.
The next Thursday. A group project went badly; nobody picked her. She came home, didn't change out of her uniform and logged straight in. It wasn't even that fun anymore, not like the first night. It was just quiet inside the game. That quiet was what she wanted.

qa.q: Where did Rashmi eat lunch at the new school?
qa.a: On the library steps, pretending to read.

qa.q: What did Rashmi want from the game by the next Thursday, if not fun?
qa.a: It gave her quiet and relief from the loneliness and hurt of being left out, which she wanted more than any thrill.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this early stage?
qa.a: An adult like Mummy could notice the long hours and the uniform still on, and gently ask about the new school, so Rashmi has someone besides the game to turn to.

qa.q: What might Yash be experiencing during these games?
qa.a: Yash probably just enjoys playing with an old friend and may not know how lonely Rashmi feels at the new school.

grounding: Shows a lonely teenager at a new school finding that long gaming sessions quiet the loneliness, with relief rather than fun drawing her back.

passage:
Dilnaz, you asked why I get so worried when you go quiet. So let me tell you your Zeenat Khala's story.
When I was sixteen, Abbu lost his job, and our house in Lucknow became all shouting and silences. I felt as if I was holding my breath all day.
One evening on the roof, an older girl from the next building offered me a cigarette. I took it mostly out of curiosity. It tasted awful. But for those few minutes, sitting up there, I wasn't inside the shouting. My shoulders came down.
That was the dangerous part, beta. Not the taste. The relief.
Within a month I was going up to the roof every evening, not because I liked it, but because it was the only place I felt I could breathe. It took me years, and a lot of help, to stop.
So if you ever feel like you're holding your breath, come and tell me first.

qa.q: What happened at home when Zeenat was sixteen?
qa.a: Abbu lost his job, and the house in Lucknow became all shouting and silences.

qa.q: Why does Zeenat call the relief 'the dangerous part'?
qa.a: The cigarette tasted awful, but it eased her stress at home, and that relief is what pulled her back to the roof every evening.

qa.q: What does Zeenat offer Dilnaz, and why does it matter at this stage?
qa.a: She invites Dilnaz to come and talk first whenever things feel too much, so there is a safe person to turn to before a habit becomes the way to cope.

qa.q: What might Dilnaz feel hearing this story from Khala?
qa.a: Dilnaz may be surprised that Khala once struggled like this, and may understand that the worry comes from care rather than suspicion.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a teenager whose first cigarette brought relief from stress at home, and how that relief began a coping habit.

passage:
Note for our meeting with the school counsellor. Written by Gurleen Kaur, Kishore's mother, 12 March
Over two months Kishore has dropped his old cricket friends, started coming home late with new boys we don't know, and keeps his phone face down. He snaps if asked anything.
Last Friday I found a vape in his school bag. I shouted, took his phone and grounded him for a month. He locked himself in his room and has not spoken to me properly since. That did not work.
On Tuesday I tried again, calmer. I made his favourite rajma and asked, "What does it do for you? I really want to know."
After a long silence he said, "It's the only time my head stops buzzing about boards."
We talked for almost an hour, the first real conversation in months.
What I would like from this meeting: help with his exam stress, and ideas for how we keep talking.

qa.q: What did Gurleen find in Kishore's school bag?
qa.a: She found a vape.

qa.q: What does Kishore's answer about his head 'buzzing' reveal about why he vapes?
qa.a: It suggests he uses it for relief from worry about the boards, not mainly for fun.

qa.q: Which approach opened honest talk, and why?
qa.a: The calm Tuesday conversation over rajma, with a real question about what vaping does for him, because it invited him to explain rather than defend himself.

qa.q: How might Kishore have experienced the shouting compared with the Tuesday talk?
qa.a: The shouting and grounding likely felt like an attack, so he shut himself away; the Tuesday question felt like real interest, which made it safe to admit the stress.

grounding: Shows a parent whose alarmed punishment shuts a teen down, and whose calm curiosity about what vaping does for him opens honest talk.

passage:
Wednesday night
Found Tanvir gaming at 2:40 am again, headphones on, lit blue by the screen. My first thought was to yank the charger out of the wall. I actually had my hand on it.
Then I remembered how that went in January: he screamed, I screamed, and he just played at his friend Neil's house instead.
So tonight I sat on the edge of his bed and waited for the round to end. Then I asked, "What does it give you, beta? Honestly."
He looked at me as if I'd grown two heads. Then he said, "When I'm playing, nobody at school is laughing at me."
I didn't know anyone was laughing at him. I didn't know any of it.
I said, "That's not your fault, beta. Thank you for telling me. Let's talk more tomorrow after school. Sleep now?" He actually nodded.
Morning: call his class teacher about the teasing. Keep my voice calm.
Damini

qa.q: What time did Damini find Tanvir gaming?
qa.a: At 2:40 am.

qa.q: Why did Damini stop with a hand on the charger?
qa.a: Damini remembered that yanking it in January led to screaming and Tanvir playing at Neil's house instead, so punishment hadn't worked.

qa.q: What does Damini plan for the morning, and why is it a good next step?
qa.a: To call the class teacher about the teasing and keep a calm voice, which deals with the reason Tanvir escapes into games, not just the gaming.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Tanvir to be asked 'What does it give you?'
qa.a: He may have been surprised to be asked instead of scolded, and it gave him a chance to admit that classmates were laughing at him.

grounding: Illustrates a parent resisting a punishing reaction to late-night gaming and asking calmly what it gives the teen, which reveals the teasing behind it.

passage:
By the third month, the small bets on the phone game did nothing for Nitin anymore. Only bigger ones made his chest go loose the way the first ones had.
He played in the back of Baba's cloth shop in Jalna, between customers, the screen turned to the wall. When Baba asked where two thousand rupees from the till had gone, Nitin said a supplier had come for an advance. The lie came out so easily that it scared him.
That evening Hafsa messaged: "Volleyball at the maidan? You haven't come in weeks." He wrote back, "Busy with shop accounts." He wasn't.
He lay on the terrace with the phone on his chest, feeling filthy about the till money, and the feeling was so heavy that the only thing that lifted it was one more bet. Dimly, he knew this was going round in a circle.

In September, one glass of wine after a long library day had been enough to bring Selin's shoulders down. By December in Rotterdam it took much more, and the calm came later and left sooner.
She began buying from a corner shop two streets away, where nobody from her building went, and kept the bottles in her wardrobe behind her winter boots. When her flatmate Lars asked why she'd missed choir again, she said she had a group assignment. When her mother asked on a video call why she needed extra money this month, she said textbooks.
Each lie sat in her stomach like a stone. At night, alone, she felt ashamed of the wardrobe, and that shame was exactly the feeling she reached for the bottle to quiet.
She had loved choir. She couldn't remember the last song they'd sung.

qa.a: In her wardrobe behind her winter boots.

qa.q: What might Lars be noticing from the outside?
qa.a: Lars sees a flatmate who keeps missing choir with excuses and may sense something is wrong without knowing what is hidden.

grounding: Illustrates needing more alcohol for the same calm, hiding it, lying about money and time, dropping choir, and shame from secrecy driving more drinking.
